title: Thermo Fisher Patches Flaw That Exposed 30 Years of DNA Evidence to Tampering
excerpt: A vulnerability in the software used by most US crime labs allowed DNA analysis files to be altered without a trace, researchers found. The company issued a high-severity bulletin after The Wall Street Journal's inquiry.
body:
• Forensic researchers discovered that DNA analysis files produced by Thermo Fisher's crime-lab machines could be altered without leaving any trace of tampering
  • The vulnerability has existed since 1995, but AI tools like Anthropic's Claude now make exploitation far easier — one researcher modified a file in 45 minutes
  • Thermo Fisher issued a high-severity security bulletin and released a software update with digital signatures after being contacted by The Wall Street Journal
  • The flaw affects the more than 200 US labs handling forensic DNA, paternity tests and criminal evidence, though no known exploitation has occurred

A security vulnerability in Thermo Fisher Scientific's DNA analysis software left three decades of forensic crime files open to undetectable manipulation, according to research by a group of forensic and computer scientists reported by The Wall Street Journal.

The researchers demonstrated that using widely available AI tools, they could alter the digital files produced by crime-lab DNA scanners without leaving any trace of tampering. The flaw is believed to have existed in the file formats generated by Thermo Fisher's machines since 1995, but the rise of generative AI has dramatically lowered the technical barrier to exploitation.

How the Vulnerability Works

Nathan Adams, a systems engineer at Ohio-based DNA consulting firm Forensic Bioinformatics, began testing the issue earlier this year using a public dataset of DNA files. Using Anthropic's Claude, Adams said his first successful file modification took about 45 minutes.

https://x.com/Dinosn/status/2084205567229202848

In a demonstration observed by the Journal, Adams's code combined the scans of two individual DNA profiles into a new file that appeared untouched since 2015. The modified file raised no red flags when processed through the analysis software that most crime labs use.

"Effectively, what we have are data files that are legitimately referred to as the gold standard of forensic science that lack the same level of tamper-evident markings that we require for a paper bag."

— Laura Gaydosh Combs, University of New Haven

Some file types carry a higher level of encryption, but Adams discovered that a decryption key had been available on the internet for years. In theory, a sophisticated attacker with local or remote access to a lab's servers could add or remove DNA profiles from crime-scene evidence, creating the impression a suspect was not present or that an innocent person was.

Thermo Fisher's Response

The company privately acknowledged the vulnerability in July after researchers flagged it in May. After the Journal contacted Thermo Fisher, it issued a security bulletin on Friday labelled "high severity" that warned of "a risk for nearly undetectable modification" of certain files "if laboratory controls are circumvented."

In a statement, the company said it had been "working closely with the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Agency" and had released a software update implementing digital signatures "to add an extra layer of protection that moving forward will help customers verify that data files have not been modified."

Thermo Fisher also told customers there were no known instances of the vulnerability being exploited.

Systemic Gaps in Forensic Science

The discovery highlights broader weaknesses in the security infrastructure of forensic science. There is no central national regulator for forensic labs in the United States, leading to a patchwork of security measures across the more than 200 facilities that handle everything from criminal evidence to paternity tests.

"Lessons learned from other industries haven't been imported into forensic science in a serious way. We've been behind the ball for so long."

— Sarah Chu, Director of Policy and Reform, Perlmutter Center for Legal Justice

The vulnerability does not affect physical DNA material submitted for testing, only the digital files produced after scanning. But defence attorneys regularly challenge DNA collection and analysis in criminal trials, and this revelation could open new avenues for legal challenges to existing convictions.

Implications Beyond US Borders

While the immediate focus is on US crime labs, Thermo Fisher's DNA analysis equipment is used globally, including in India's expanding forensic infrastructure. India has been building forensic capacity under the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, which increases the role of forensic evidence in criminal investigations. The vulnerability raises questions about whether labs worldwide have adequate cybersecurity protocols for evidence that can determine guilt or innocence.

For diaspora communities navigating legal systems in multiple countries, the integrity of forensic evidence is not an abstract concern. The case underscores the need for international standards in forensic data security, particularly as AI tools continue to lower the barrier for sophisticated digital manipulation.
